results.title: Measurement Invariance of Neuropsychological Tests in Diverse Older Persons - PMC
results.content: Principal component analysis (PCA) was widely used in earlier studies to investigate measurement invariance; for example, to examine of the construct validity of intelligence tests across groups defined by race/ethnicity (e.g. Chastain & Joe, 1987; Kaufman, McLean, & Reynolds, 1991) and language (e.g. Drago, Daum, & Canavan, 1991; Gomez, Piedmont, & Fleming, 1992; Insua, 1983; Laicardi, Frustaci, & Lauriola, 1996; Orsini & Laicardi, 2000). PCA has limitations in evaluating measurement invariance (Borsboom, 2006), and more rigorous methods based on confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) have been recommended more recently for comparing the factor structure of cognitive tests and batteries across diverse groups (e.g. Geary & Whitworth, 1988; Grégoire, 2004; Pedraza, et al., 2005; Widaman & Reise, 1997). ### Data Analysis #### Overview Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was used to evaluate the dimensional structure of the 16 SENAS measures and to test measurement invariance across the groups defined by ethnicity and language. Configural invariance occurs when the same dimensional structure is applicable in the different groups, though formal parameters like loadings (the strength of the relationship of the test with the underlying factor) and intercepts (the expected test score when the factor score is 0.0, i.e. at the sample average) might be different. This study found five dimensions that reasonably explained covariance among the 16 component measures from the SENAS in four different groups: African Americans, Caucasians, and English- and Spanish-speaking Hispanics. While a five factor model based on the previous studies fit well in the African American sample, invariance of the measurement model was not directly tested across the three studies. Results were similar for the Fluency factor, though there were minor differences in Phonemic Fluency intercepts suggesting that this task is harder for Hispanics, especially Spanish speakers, in the sense that test scores for a given level of ability would be expected to be somewhat higher (about 0.25–0.33 s.d.) in African Americans and Caucasians. This is sufficient to establish a common metric that makes it appropriate to compare factor means across groups; comparison of means of individual tests defining this factor is appropriate except that the Verbal Expression score in African Americans and the Verbal Conceptual Thinking score in Spanish administration Hispanics likely are not on the same scale as these scores in other groups.

results.title: Okan Bulut: Testing for Measurement Invariance in R
results.content: In this post, I demonstrate how to test for measurement invariance (i.e., configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance) of an instrument using R. To test for measurement invariance, we need to estimate and compare increasingly constrained confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) models with each other:. * **Scalar invariance model:** A constrained version of the metric model where both the factor loadings and intercepts are assumed to be equal across groups. * **Strict invariance model:** A constrained version of the scalar model where the factor loadings, intercepts, and residual variances are fixed across groups. We will use `dplyr` (Wickham et al., 2020) for organizing data, `corrplot` (Wei & Simko, 2017) for visualizing the correlation matrix of the items, `lavaan` (Rosseel, 2012) to estimate multi-group CFA models, and `semTools` (Jorgensen et al., 2020) to run model comparison tests. Despite good model-fit indices presented in the rest of the output, the statistically significant result suggests that there is a lack of scalar invariance for the Financial Well-Being Scale.
